analysis.one_liner: Restores a shield protecting credit rating agencies from investor lawsuits over their ratings.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee advanced the bill 31-19 in July 2011, but it never received a House floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal a provision of the 2010 Dodd-Frank financial reform law (section 939G) that wiped out an old SEC rule (Rule 436G) [S2] [S4]. That rule had exempted credit ratings from rating agencies from being treated as part of the registration statement a company files when selling securities to the public [S2] [S3]. Restoring the rule would put rating agencies back behind a shield: an investor who lost money on a bond with an inflated rating could not sue the agency the way it can sue other experts, like accountants, whose work appears in that filing. The bill was aimed chiefly at the market for asset-backed securities, where Dodd-Frank's liability change threatened to keep rating agencies from allowing their ratings in bond prospectuses.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit rating agencies such as Moody's, Standard & Poor's, and Fitch, which would regain exemption from expert-style legal liability for ratings used in securities registration statements. Banks and firms that package loans into asset-backed securities would also benefit, since restoring the rule keeps agency ratings available in the bond documents investors rely on.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 939G of the Dodd-Frank Act, thereby restoring SEC Rule 436G, which exempts ratings from nationally recognized statistical rating organizations from being considered part of a securities registration statement [S2] [S3] [S4].

By keeping ratings out of the registration statement, the restored rule would free rating agencies from the 'expert' legal liability that section 939G had exposed them to, removing the agencies' stated reason for barring their ratings from asset-backed securities filings [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Investors in asset-backed securities, including the mutual funds and retirement accounts that hold them, who would lose the ability to sue a rating agency as an 'expert' for publishing an inflated rating that appeared in a bond prospectus.

drawbacks.text: Restoring the exemption would remove one of the few ways investors could hold rating agencies financially accountable for sloppy or inflated ratings of bonds, the same ratings that failed during the 2008 financial crisis [S2] [S4].

A good-faith objection runs the other way: without the shield, rating agencies had signaled they would withdraw consent for their ratings to appear in asset-backed securities registration statements, which could freeze the market that finances car loans, credit cards, and student loans. The bill was framed as fixing that, though Dodd-Frank's separate temporary arrangement (section 939F) already allowed ratings to be included without agency consent, blunting the urgency of a full repeal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated benefit - keeping rating agencies from pulling out of asset-backed securities filings - was already largely addressed by the temporary arrangement Congress wrote into Dodd-Frank itself, so the bill's main real-world effect was to permanently shield a small, concentrated industry from lawsuits. The cost falls on bond investors, who lost the most from inflated pre-crisis ratings and would lose their strongest legal remedy.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee passed it 31-19 in July 2011 and placed it on the Union Calendar in August 2011, but it was never brought to the House floor for a vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Stivers introduced the bill on April 14, 2011, with Reps. Jim Renacci and Hansen Clarke as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S4] [S5] [S6].
The subcommittee on Capital Markets forwarded the bill to the full committee on a vote of 18-14 in May 2011 [S6].

The full Financial Services Committee ordered the bill reported 31-19 on July 20, 2011, and reported it without amendment on August 12, 2011 (H. Rept. 112-196), placing it on the Union Calendar [S3] [S4] [S6].
The bill never received a House floor vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors in asset-backed securities, who kept the ability to sue rating agencies over ratings used in bond registration statements, since the agencies' push for a full liability shield never became law. The rating agencies' effort failed, though they had also secured the temporary arrangement in Dodd-Frank that addressed the immediate market problem.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Investors, who kept recourse against rating agencies

sides.party_line_note: The bill's original and added sponsors were Republicans with one Democratic cosponsor (Hansen Clarke of Michigan), but the votes to move it out of subcommittee (18-14) and full committee (31-19) split largely on party lines, with Republicans in favor and Democrats opposed.

industries.industry: Credit rating agencies (NRSROs such as Moody's, S&P, and Fitch)
industries.note: The bill's sole purpose was to restore these agencies' exemption from 'expert' legal liability for ratings used in securities registration statements. The agencies gain by shedding lawsuit risk; investors lose the ability to recover for inflated ratings.

industries.industry: Bankers and issuers of asset-backed securities
industries.note: Restoring Rule 436G keeps agency ratings available in asset-backed securities prospectuses, keeping the securitization market that finances loans running. The gain is real, but the same shield that helps the market removes investor recourse.

Under this bill, investors could no longer sue a rating agency as an expert for a rating that appeared in a registration statement, leaving pension funds and individual savers with weaker recourse against overstated ratings.
